subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Local Group
description: Learn The Local Group in one minute.

hook.text: Our Milky Way belongs to the Local Group—a collection of about 80 galaxies spanning 10 million light-years.

buildup.text: The two largest members are the Milky Way and Andromeda. The third largest, Triangulum, is much smaller.

discovery.text: Most members are tiny dwarf galaxies orbiting the two giants. Many were discovered only in the last two decades.

twist.text: The Local Group is gravitationally bound—its members orbit each other rather than flying apart with the expanding universe.

climax.text: In billions of years, the Local Group will merge into a single giant galaxy as smaller members are consumed.

punchline.text: Eighty galaxies bound together. Our cosmic neighborhood, destined to merge.

quiz.question: What is the Local Group?
options: A gravitationally bound collection of about 80 galaxies including the Milky Way
The closest 10 stars to our solar system
A cluster of galaxies billions of light-years away

details.summary: The Local Group is the collection of over 80 galaxies gravitationally bound together that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda (M31), the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), and dozens of dwarf galaxies.
details.whyItMatters: The Local Group is our cosmic neighborhood — the only place where individual stars in other galaxies can be resolved. Studying it in detail provides the foundation for understanding galaxy groups throughout the universe.
takeaways: Dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda

faq.question: Which is larger — the Milky Way or Andromeda?
faq.answer: This has been debated. Andromeda appears to have more stars and a larger disk diameter. However, recent studies suggest the Milky Way's total mass (including dark matter) may be comparable or even slightly greater.

faq.question: Will the Local Group always exist?
faq.answer: In the near cosmic future, the Local Group will merge into a single large galaxy over the next 5-10 billion years (starting with Milky Way-Andromeda). Meanwhile, dark energy is pushing other galaxy groups away.
